title: The Dolphins, the Whales, and the Sprat
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: The Dolphins quarrelled with the Whales, and before very long they began fighting with one another. The battle was very fierce, and had lasted some time without any sign of coming to an end, when a Sprat thought that perhaps he could stop it; so he stepped in and tried to persuade them to give up fighting and make friends. But one of the Dolphins said to him contemptuously, "We would rather go on fighting till we're all killed than be reconciled by a Sprat like you!"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who does the Dolphins quarrel with?
options: The Sharks
A group of fishermen
The Whales
A school of Sprats

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the battle between the Dolphins and Whales develop over time?
options: It becomes very fierce and lasts a long time with no end in sight
It ends quickly once both sides grow tired
It is interrupted almost immediately by a storm
It never actually turns into real fighting

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who steps in to try to stop the fighting?
options: A larger fish from another sea
One of the older Dolphins
A passing group of sailors
A Sprat

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sprat try to persuade the Dolphins and Whales to do?
options: Divide the sea between them peacefully
Give up fighting and make friends
Wait until a judge could settle the matter
Fight only during certain hours of the day

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Dolphin respond to the Sprat's offer?
options: With gratitude, agreeing to stop at once
With confusion, asking who sent him
With contempt, saying they would rather fight till they're all killed
With laughter, thinking it was a joke

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Dolphin say he would prefer over being reconciled by the Sprat?
options: To go on fighting till they're all killed
To ask a bigger fish to mediate instead
To leave the sea entirely
To fight only the Whales he respects

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Dolphin reject the Sprat's help so scornfully?
options: He believes the Sprat is secretly allied with the Whales
He thinks the Sprat is trying to steal credit for ending the war
He does not understand what the Sprat is offering to do
He considers the Sprat too small and insignificant to have any standing to intervene

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Dolphin's reply suggest about how pride can affect a conflict?
options: It always leads to a quick and decisive victory
It can make combatants reject a reasonable peace simply because of who is offering it
It has no real effect on how long a conflict lasts
It only matters when the mediator is powerful

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "contemptuously" mean in "said to him contemptuously"?
options: In a fearful, hesitant way
In a friendly, welcoming way
In a scornful, dismissive way
In a confused, uncertain way

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Those caught up in a fierce quarrel may reject peace simply because it is offered by someone they consider beneath them
Small creatures should never attempt to resolve conflicts between larger ones
Wars between sea creatures are impossible to end peacefully
Sprats are wiser than both Dolphins and Whales

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the ongoing battle eventually turn into?
options: A truce negotiated by a third party
A race across the open sea
A contest judged by the Sprat
Fighting between the two groups

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sprat do besides simply speaking to them?
options: He swims away to find reinforcements
He steps in between the two sides
He waits until the fighting ends on its own
He reports the fight to a higher authority

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Dolphin call the Sprat while refusing his help?
options: "A foolish little fish"
"An unwanted stranger"
"A Sprat like you"
"A coward from the shallows"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the length and ferocity of the battle suggest about the two sides' willingness to compromise?
options: Neither side seems inclined to stop, even before the Sprat's offer is refused
Both sides were already close to reaching a peaceful agreement
One side had clearly already won by the time the Sprat arrived
The battle had actually ended before the Sprat intervened

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the size difference between the Sprat and the fighting animals matter to the story's point?
options: It shows that only large animals can ever end a war
It proves that small creatures are always ignored in any dispute
It suggests the Sprat was too weak to physically separate the fighters
It shows that the value of an offer of peace should not depend on the size of the one offering it

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "reconciled" mean in "be reconciled by a Sprat like you"?
options: Defeated in open battle
Brought back into friendly terms
Separated permanently
Placed under new leadership

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Sprat successfully makes peace between the Dolphins and the Whales
The Dolphins and Whales end their battle before the Sprat arrives
A small Sprat's offer to end a fierce battle between Dolphins and Whales is scornfully refused
The Sprat joins the battle on the side of the Whales
